title: Die Geschichte vom Hanns Guck-in-die-Luft
source: Heinrich Hoffmann, Der Struwwelpeter, Rütten & Loening, Frankfurt am Main, 564. Auflage — the canonical later text in modernized spelling (via Project Gutenberg #24571). Fresh Lectorium translation from the German.
about: Hanns walks to school with his eyes on the roofs and the swallows and never on the ground — first into a dog, then into the river. The rescue is prompt and matter-of-fact, two men with poles, and the whole of his punishment is standing there dripping while three little fish laugh at him. Nothing is lost in the end but the schoolbag, already floating off downstream.

sentences.t:
Wenn der Hanns zur Schule ging,
stets sein Blick am Himmel hing.
sentences.l:
When the Hanns to school went,
always his gaze on the sky hung.
sentences.i:
Whenever Hanns walked to school,
his eyes were fixed on the sky.
sentences.n: »wenn« with a past tense means ‘whenever’ — the habit, not one particular morning. »sein Blick hing am Himmel« is the German picture: the gaze *hangs* on the sky (»hängen an« + dative) where English would say it was fixed there. »stets« = ‘always,’ old-fashioned now. And »der Hanns« — the article before the name once again.

sentences.t:
Nach den Dächern, Wolken, Schwalben
schaut er aufwärts allenthalben.
sentences.l:
Toward the roofs, clouds, swallows
looks he upwards everywhere.
sentences.i:
At the roofs, the clouds, the swallows
he looks up, everywhere he goes.
sentences.n: »schauen nach« = ‘to look towards, gaze at,’ and the whole »nach«-phrase is thrown to the front, which pushes the verb into second place and the subject behind it. »allenthalben« is an old word for ‘everywhere, on every side,’ long out of use. Note the tense slipping from past (»ging«, »hing«) to present (»schaut«): the storyteller steps into the scene, as this book does constantly.

sentences.t:
Vor die eignen Füße dicht,
ja, da sah der Bursche nicht,
also daß ein jeder ruft:
»Seht den Hanns Guck-in-die-Luft!«
sentences.l:
In front of the own feet close,
yes, there saw the lad not,
so that each one calls:
“See the Hanns Look-in-the-Air!”
sentences.i:
But right in front of his own feet —
there the lad never looked,
so that everyone calls out:
“Look at Hanns Look-in-the-Air!”
sentences.n: »dicht« (‘close, right up against’) trails after its phrase for the rhyme; »eignen« is »eigenen« clipped. The place is named first and then picked up again by »da« (‘there’) — spoken German spotlights a thing this way before saying anything about it. »also daß« = ‘so that’ (»also« is the old ‘thus,’ nothing to do with English ‘also’). »ein jeder« = ‘every single one.’ The nickname is a whole command turned into a name: ‘look-into-the-air.’

»Kam ein Hund …« with nothing in front of it is verse shorthand for ‘there came a dog’ — the verb simply opens the sentence. »daher gerannt kommen« = ‘to come running along’: German says the manner with a participle and leaves »kommen« to carry the sentence, where English puts ‘came’ first and ‘running’ after. »Hännslein« is Hanns with the -lein diminutive, ‘little Hanns’ — the poem shrinks his name just as the danger arrives, and shrinks it again to »Hännschen« a few lines later. »unverwandt« = ‘without turning away, fixedly.’

sentences.t:
Niemand ruft:
»Hanns! gib acht, der Hund ist nah!«
Was geschah?
sentences.l:
Nobody calls:
“Hanns! give heed, the dog is near!”
What happened?
sentences.i:
Nobody calls out:
“Hanns! watch out, the dog is close!”
And what happened?
sentences.n: »acht geben« = ‘to pay heed, watch out’ (printed lowercase »acht« in this edition, like »in acht nehmen« in the Friederich). The cold word is »Niemand«: the same street that had a name ready for him has no warning. »Was geschah?« is the storyteller turning to the listener for a beat before the crash.

sentences.t:
Bauz, perdauz! – da liegen zwei,
Hund und Hännschen nebenbei.
sentences.l:
Bang, crash! – there lie two,
dog and little-Hanns side by side.
sentences.i:
Bang, wallop! — and there lie the two of them,
dog and little Hanns, side by side.
sentences.n: »Bauz!« is the crash from the Daumenlutscher again; »perdauz« is a nonsense word coined to double it. The sentence names nobody until the end: first »da liegen zwei« — ‘there lie two’ — and only then who the two are. »nebenbei« here means ‘one beside the other,’ its old spatial sense; in modern German it has drifted to ‘incidentally, on the side.’

sentences.t:
Einst ging er an Ufers Rand
mit der Mappe in der Hand.
sentences.l:
Once went he at shore’s edge
with the satchel in the hand.
sentences.i:
One day he was walking along the water’s edge
with his schoolbag in his hand.
sentences.n: »einst« = ‘once, one day.’ »an Ufers Rand« is the poetic genitive with the article dropped — »an des Ufers Rand«, ‘at the bank’s edge.’ »die Mappe« is the flat satchel a schoolchild carried books in — and »in der Hand«, the definite article again where English wants ‘his.’

sentences.t:
Nach dem blauen Himmel hoch
sah er, wo die Schwalbe flog,
also daß er kerzengrad
immer mehr zum Flusse trat.
sentences.l:
Toward the blue sky high
looked he, where the swallow flew,
so that he candle-straight
ever more to the river stepped.
sentences.i:
He was looking up at the blue sky,
where the swallow was flying,
and so, bolt upright,
he stepped nearer and nearer the river.
sentences.n: »kerzengrad« (»kerzengerade«) is literally ‘candle-straight,’ the everyday German for bolt upright — and it does double duty here: he holds himself straight, and he walks straight on. »immer mehr« = ‘more and more, nearer and nearer.’ »zum Flusse« keeps the old dative -e. »also daß« joins cause to consequence again, exactly as in the first stanza.

sentences.t:
Und die Fischlein in der Reih
sind erstaunt sehr, alle drei.
sentences.l:
And the little-fishes in the row
are astonished greatly, all three.
sentences.i:
And the little fish in their row
are astonished indeed, all three of them.
sentences.n: »das Fischlein« — the -lein diminutive again, ‘little fish’ (the plural looks the same). »in der Reih« is »in der Reihe« clipped for the rhyme: the three of them lined up in a row, just as Hoffmann draws them. »erstaunt sehr« is plain »sehr erstaunt« with the two words swapped to fit the line — and this »sehr« is the ordinary modern one, strengthening an adjective, not the old ‘sorely’ of »da schreit der Konrad sehr«. The fish are the poem’s audience, and they get the last laugh.

sentences.t:
Noch ein Schritt! und plumps! der Hanns
stürzt hinab kopfüber ganz! –
sentences.l:
One more step! and plop! the Hanns
plunges down head-over entirely! –
sentences.i:
One step more! and splash! — down goes Hanns,
head over heels, the whole way! —
sentences.n: »plumps!« is the sound of something falling into water. »hinabstürzen« (‘to plunge down’) is separable, and here the »hinab« follows straight after the verb, with »kopfüber ganz« piling on behind it — head over heels, and all the way. The dash at the end of the line is Hoffmann’s own: a held breath before the fish.

sentences.t:
Die drei Fischlein, sehr erschreckt,
haben sich sogleich versteckt.
sentences.l:
The three little-fishes, very frightened,
have themselves at once hidden.
sentences.i:
The three little fish, badly startled,
hid themselves at once.
sentences.n: »sich verstecken« is reflexive — ‘to hide oneself’ — with the »sich« early and the participle »versteckt« waiting at the end. »sogleich« = ‘at once, straight away,’ old-fashioned. German uses the perfect (»haben … versteckt«) where English simply says ‘hid.’

sentences.t:
Doch zum Glück da kommen zwei
Männer aus der Näh herbei,
und die haben ihn mit Stangen
aus dem Wasser aufgefangen.
sentences.l:
But luckily there come two
men from nearby hither,
and those have him with poles
out of the water caught.
sentences.i:
But luckily two men
come up from close at hand,
and they, with poles,
have fished him out of the water.
sentences.n: »zum Glück« = ‘luckily, as luck would have it.’ The line break falls inside the phrase — »zwei« ending one line and »Männer« opening the next — so the number arrives before you know what there are two of. »herbeikommen« is separable: »kommen … herbei«, ‘come up to the spot.’ »die« opening the third line is the demonstrative again, ‘those two.’ »auffangen« is to catch something falling or drifting; »aus der Näh« is »Nähe« clipped.

sentences.t:
Seht! nun steht der triefend naß!
Ei, das ist ein schlechter Spaß!
sentences.l:
See! now stands that one dripping wet!
Oh, that is a poor joke!
sentences.i:
Look! there he stands, dripping wet!
Well, that is a poor sort of joke!
sentences.n: »der« standing alone as the subject is the demonstrative ‘he, that one there’ — the verse pointing at the picture. »triefend naß« = ‘dripping wet,’ the participle used as an intensifier. »Ei!« is a mild old exclamation, ‘oh, well now.’ »ein schlechter Spaß« is ‘a poor joke, no fun at all’ — the narrator’s dry understatement, with the boy still standing in a puddle.

sentences.t:
Wasser läuft dem armen Wicht
aus den Haaren ins Gesicht,
aus den Kleidern, von den Armen,
und es friert ihn zum Erbarmen.
sentences.l:
Water runs to-the poor wretch
out of the hair into the face,
out of the clothes, from the arms,
and it freezes him to pity.
sentences.i:
Water runs out of the poor creature’s hair
and into his face,
out of his clothes, off his arms,
and he is freezing, pitiful to see.
sentences.n: »dem armen Wicht« is the dative of the person it happens to — ‘the water runs, to his cost, out of the hair into the face’ — which is how German says ‘his hair, his face’ without a possessive anywhere in sight. »der Wicht« is a poor creature, a wretch (the word behind English ‘wight’), and it is said here with sympathy. »es friert ihn« is impersonal, ‘it freezes him’ = ‘he is freezing,’ with the person in the accusative. »zum Erbarmen« = ‘pitifully,’ literally ‘to the point of pity.’

sentences.t:
Doch die Fischlein alle drei,
schwimmen hurtig gleich herbei;
sentences.l:
But the little-fishes all three
swim briskly at once hither;
sentences.i:
But the three little fish
come swimming briskly up at once;
sentences.n: »herbeischwimmen« — the same »herbei« the two men arrived with, and separable in the same way: »schwimmen … herbei«. »hurtig« = ‘brisk, nimble,’ old-fashioned. »gleich« here means ‘right away,’ not ‘alike.’

sentences.t:
streckens Köpflein aus der Flut,
lachen, daß man's hören tut,
lachen fort noch lange Zeit.
sentences.l:
stretch-the little-head out of the flood,
laugh, that one it hear does,
laugh on still a long time.
sentences.i:
they poke their little heads out of the water,
laughing so that you can hear it,
laughing on for a long time after.
sentences.n: »streckens« is »strecken 's«, that is »strecken das Köpflein« — the article swallowed into the verb the way speech runs words together (»wie’s« in the Zappel-Philipp). And the little head stays singular for all three of them, where English wants a plural. »daß man’s hören tut« uses »tun« as a bare helper — ‘that one does hear it’ — a folksy spoken turn that survives in dialect. »fortlachen« = ‘to laugh on, keep laughing’: the same »fort« that took the mother out of the house.

sentences.t: Und die Mappe schwimmt schon weit.
sentences.l: And the satchel swims already far.
sentences.i: And the schoolbag is already floating far away.
sentences.n: »schwimmen« is both ‘swim’ and ‘float,’ so the fish and the satchel take the same verb within four lines of each other. Nobody goes after it, and the poem stops there: three fish laughing, and the bag well downstream.
